hook.line: A deduction game: find a hidden row of colours from nothing but hits and blows. A pencil-and-paper guessing game became a board of coloured pegs.
hook.say: Hello, detective! Let's crack the history of Hit & Blow together.

ch.t: From pencil and paper to coloured pegs
ch.say: Hiding an answer and guessing it is a very old game.
p: Bulls and Cows, a pencil-and-paper game of guessing a secret number, is said to be a century old or more. A right digit in the right place is a “bull”; a right digit in the wrong place is a “cow”. Around 1970 a computer version called MOO became a craze on the computer of the University of Cambridge in England.

In 1970 Mordecai Meirowitz, an Israeli postmaster and telecommunications expert, turned the digits into coloured pegs on a board. Invicta Plastics of Leicester, England, bought the rights, refined the game and launched it in 1971 as Mastermind — a hit sold all over the world.

ch.say: The pins are your only clues. Time to deduce!
ch.cap: Colours (4 of 6). The pins right of each row count hits (lime) and blows (white). The light on the left shows whose turn it was
p: Set four pegs in a row as your guess, and pins come back comparing it with the answer: a lime hit for each peg with the right colour in the right place, a white blow for each right colour in the wrong place. They never say which peg is which.
Here two players take turns cracking the same answer. Your rival’s pins are clues for you too — the first to score all hits wins.

ch.say: Digits, letters, shapes — there are many ways to play the guessing game.
